content.text: "Cross-platform" isn't one technology. Flutter compiles Dart to machine code and draws its own UI, React Native drives the platform's real views from JavaScript, and Kotlin Multiplatform compiles shared Kotlin into native binaries while the UI can stay native. Each has real costs, but "always slower and unable to do serious apps" isn't a fair summary of any of them. Decide with your requirements and measurements, not with a slogan.

A startup plans its first mobile app. In the kickoff, the tech lead says, "Cross-platform is slow; every serious app is native," and nobody argues. The plan becomes two codebases and two teams. Six months later the Android app is two features behind iOS, every bug is fixed twice, and nobody ever measured the slowness the decision was built on, or even asked which cross-platform technology the sentence was about.
The common misconception
The belief: cross-platform apps are always slower and less capable than native ones, so any serious app must be built with Swift and Kotlin from day one.

It has real roots. Some cross-platform approaches do render inside web views; Flutter's own FAQ defines itself against them, saying it "doesn't rely on web browser views or system-provided platform widgets." Intuition adds the rest: any layer between your code and the OS must cost something. And some costs are real, as we'll see. The half-truth is that "cross-platform" covers technologies that work in completely different ways, and a verdict formed on one of them says little about the others.
What actually happens
Three different machines under one label

items.text: to native machine code in release builds; the FAQ says it runs "without an interpreter or bridge" and that Flutter "is designed to deliver smooth 60fps and 120fps animations." The UI is drawn by Flutter's own engine rather than built from platform widgets.

content.text: None of them is a web page in a wrapper. Their trade-offs differ, so "is cross-platform slow?" has no single answer; "is this framework fast enough for this app?" does.
The frame budget belongs to the device

Android's own guide sets the bar for native apps: render each frame in under 16 ms for 60 fps, 11 ms for 90 and 8 ms for 120. Miss it by a millisecond and the frame isn't late; it's dropped, which the guide calls
jank

. Flutter aims at the same 60 and 120 fps targets. So the question is never "native or not" but "what does this app do per frame": heavy work on the main thread, expensive drawing or a badly built list drops frames in Kotlin as surely as in Dart. Android's guide lists
RecyclerView
, a native component, among the common sources of jank to check.
Reaching the platform
"Cross-platform can't use the camera, Bluetooth or the new OS feature" is the capability half of the myth. Flutter's FAQ lists the ways in: plugins from pub.dev,
platform channels
to Kotlin, Java, Swift or Objective-C, and FFI to C. When no plugin exists yet, you write that part yourself:
Kotlin Multiplatform's docs say Kotlin/Native code can access platform APIs directly, for example on iOS. React Native lets you build your own native components when the built-in ones aren't enough.
Where the real costs are
Cross-platform isn't free, and pretending otherwise leads to the opposite mistake:

rows.text: Cross-platform means a web page in a native shell
Flutter runs AOT-compiled code and draws itself; React Native creates real platform views; KMP builds native binaries
Android's docs give native apps the same 16 ms budget at 60 fps, and a frame that misses it is dropped
Plugins, platform channels and FFI in Flutter; direct platform API access in KMP on iOS
You choose once, for the whole app
Flutter can be added to an existing app as a module; KMP can share a single networking or storage module
Flutter's engine adds a few megabytes (compressed), and a new OS API may need your own platform code until a plugin covers it

blocks.title: Never compare a debug build with a release build

content.text: Flutter debug builds run Dart with a JIT compiler for hot reload; release builds are AOT-compiled. On Android, the guide warns that a debuggable build has several ART optimizations disabled. A "cross-platform is slow" verdict from a debug build on an emulator, against a release build of a native app, measures the build mode, not the technology.
It isn't all or nothing

With add-to-app, Flutter "can be integrated into your existing application piecemeal, as a module," on Android, iOS, macOS and the web: some screens in Flutter, the rest native, or even a Flutter widget inside a native screen. Kotlin Multiplatform's docs describe the same gradual path: share an isolated module such as networking or storage, then expand, or share all business logic and keep the UI native.

In our experience, the deciding factors are rarely raw speed. They're the team you have, how custom the UI is, how much of the app is deep platform integration (home-screen widgets, watch apps, background work), and how much code you already own.

blocks.title: Prototype the screen you fear most

content.text: Pick the hardest screen, such as a long feed with images or a heavy animation, build it in the candidate stack, and run it in release or profile mode on the slowest device you'll support. A day of measurements beats a month of opinions.
How to apply it in your project
Write down your targets: frame rate on the slowest device you support, startup time, download size and the platform APIs you need.
For each one, check whether a maintained plugin or library exists, and estimate the native code you'd write if not.

items.title: Measure the riskiest screen in release mode

content.text: Prototype it and profile it on real hardware. Compare release builds only.
If you already have native apps, try one Flutter screen through add-to-app, or one shared KMP module, before deciding for the whole product.
Keep the measurements with the decision, so the next "cross-platform is slow" debate starts from numbers.
Key takeaways

items.text: Flutter, React Native and Kotlin Multiplatform work in very different ways; judge the one you're considering.
The frame budget is set by the screen: native apps drop frames too when they do too much per frame.
Platform APIs are reachable through plugins, platform channels, FFI or KMP's direct access, at the cost of some native code.
The real costs are concrete: engine size, and waiting for or writing platform code when a new OS API ships.
Compare release builds on real devices, and remember you can adopt cross-platform one screen or one module at a time.
